Usually you don't need to cut it. Most gas cap tethers are attached through a small plastic loop or pin that just pulls out of the cap body or the cap's mounting clip. Look at where the tether meets the cap: if there's a tiny clip or retaining pin, gently pry it out with a flathead screwdriver or fingernail and the tether will slide free. If the tether is simply knotted or looped through a hole, pull the end through the hole. If it's firmly fused or you can't find a way to release it, cutting it with scissors or a utility knife is perfectly fine, since the tether is only a cosmetic or convenience strap and doesn't affect how the cap seals. Just be careful not to damage the cap's rubber seal or threads when prying.

A broken extraction tool stuck in a spark plug is a common problem. Options: First, try a spark plug extractor with a left-hand reverse-thread design or a tap-style extractor. Use a reverse-threaded extractor kit to grip the broken piece, or drill a small pilot hole in the center of the broken tool and tap in an easy-out (screw extractor), turning counterclockwise slowly. Apply penetrating oil and let it soak first, and heat the cylinder head gently if it's cold-stuck. Keep debris out of the cylinder by stuffing a clean rag into the spark plug hole and vacuuming around it as you work. Because the 2005 Expedition's 5.4L engine has aluminum heads and the plugs can be seized, if the tool is deeply lodged or you can't get it out without risking threads, take it to a shop that can helicoil or re-thread the head.
